fixes.explanation: That's right, baker. The man who released the goat “…must wash his clothes and bathe himself with water; afterward he may reenter the camp.” (Leviticus 16:26). Clothes first, bath too, and only THEN back into the camp. The text doesn't say why, so I'll just say it's a very thorough cleanup. I've gotten dough all over this mustache and I still only got a rag.

You got it, baker. The bull and the goat, whose blood was brought into the Most Holy Place, are taken outside the camp, “and their hides, flesh, and dung must be burned up.” (Leviticus 16:27). Hides, flesh and dung, all three named for the fire. When my oven burns a batch, I at least get a few sad crumbs. This fire is much more thorough than mine.

Enrich sounds like a day to get ahead, baker, but look at the verse. “…you shall humble yourselves and not do any work…” (Leviticus 16:29). Getting richer is the opposite of that day's whole point, which is a Sabbath of complete rest (Leviticus 16:31). The word is humble.

problems.problem: It reuses a line from the Prep cards word for word.
The line about the camp not taking the man's word invents an attitude and a reason for the washing that the passage does not give.
The hands-in-pockets comparison claims you cannot enrich anything without using your hands. That is not true, and the image does not clarify the contrast with humbling oneself.
